briefing.text: A claim about uniform versus heterogeneous in vivo chemotherapy sensitivity of engrafted tumoroids can only be tested with a per-model response variable, such as treated-versus-control tumour volume change, mRECIST class, growth curves, or IC50/AUC. Search every column and every '#' description line of all six files for terms like response, volume, growth, IC50, AUC, mouse, xenograft, engraft, mRECIST, treated or sensitivity, and name the exact column used. Whether the hypothesis sounds plausible clinically (rectal cancer response is known to vary) is not evidence either way; the label must rest on what the data columns actually contain.
briefing.reason: The deciding question is whether any response variable exists at all; without checking, teams may call True or False from prior knowledge.

briefing.text: If data_clinical_sample.txt has a THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION (or similar) column, read its description line: it records the patient's treatment before the tumoroid was derived, not how the engrafted tumoroid responded in mice. It is a potential confounder of resistance, not a measure of sensitivity, unless a paired post-treatment outcome is also present.
briefing.reason: This column is the most likely to be misread as drug-response data.

briefing.text: Genomic heterogeneity between tumoroids (mutations, CNA, TMB) is not a measure of chemotherapy sensitivity; genotype-to-chemo-response links are weak. An argument built only from data_mutations, data_cna or TMB is indirect evidence about drug response and should not by itself be used to call the sensitivity claim supported or contradicted.
briefing.reason: The data are mostly genomic, so teams may be tempted to use genomic diversity as a proxy for response.

briefing.text: The sample table mixes paired patient-tumour (-pt) and tumoroid (-tm) samples, Primary/Metastasis/Recurrence sample types, and FFPE versus Fresh preservation. Tabulate SAMPLE_ID suffixes, SAMPLE_TYPE and SPECIMEN_PRESERVATION_TYPE and count unique PATIENT_ID; analyse per patient or by matched pair rather than pooling samples.
briefing.reason: Pooling sample types double-counts patients and confounds model versus tumour in any comparison the teams run.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume the only admissible evidence is an explicit per-model in vivo response column (volume, mRECIST, IC50/AUC); neither considered whether any sample-level encoding (e.g. derivation after therapy, serial passages) could encode a treated-vs-untreated in vivo arm.

Both treat the 287 MSK-IMPACT clinical tumours (P-xxxx samples) as out of scope without stating so; the hypothesis contrasts tumoroids with 'clinical observations', and neither checked whether that clinical cohort carries any outcome/response variable.
unused_evidence: The 287 P-xxxx MSK-IMPACT rectal cancer samples (clinical comparator cohort) and their columns (SAMPLE_TYPE, MSI, TMB, TUMOR_PURITY); neither team reported tabulating what this cohort can and cannot say about clinical chemo response.

Serial/post-therapy tumoroid derivations (022 MC/PC/TNT, 025 TNT-P2m/P7m/P9m, 034MP) and their matched pre-treatment tumoroids: genomic change pre vs post therapy is not response, but neither team documented that no in vivo treatment arm is encoded in these suffixes beyond prior-therapy text.
data_patient has only SEX; no survival/response columns - confirmed implicitly but not explicitly reported by team B.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A's weakest point (suffixes like TNT/MC/PC could encode response) was argued away by interpretation rather than checked against the column description lines; Team B's weakest point (prior-therapy text misread as response) was reported, not tested. Both are low-risk.
second_readings: 'Uniform sensitivity ... unlike clinical observations' could be read as a comparison of heterogeneity between tumoroids and the clinical cohort on some shared variable (e.g. MSI/TMB/mutation profile as drivers of sensitivity); this would still be an indirect proxy, not chemo sensitivity, so it does not plausibly change the label.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed 'Not verifiable' answer highly: my own inspection found the files contain only sex, sample metadata, prior patient therapy text and genomic tables, with no in vivo or clinical response variable; the questions only ask the teams to document the clinical comparator cohort and suffix meanings explicitly.

In public cancer genomics portal sample tables for patient-derived organoid studies, does the 'therapy prior to derivation' field ever record treatment of the derived model in vivo, or only treatment of the patient before tissue collection?
questions.why: Confirms the field convention on which both teams' exclusion of the only therapy-related column rests.

findings.question: In public cancer genomics portal sample tables for patient-derived organoid studies, does the 'therapy prior to derivation' field ever record treatment of the derived model in vivo, or only treatment of the patient before tissue collection?
findings.answer: By the conventions I could read, the field records only the patient's treatment before tissue collection, not in vivo treatment of the derived model. Cell Model Passports keeps 'Sample Treatment (Prior Treatment)', defined as any therapy the patient received before sampling, separate from 'Model Treatment', defined as treatment during or after model derivation. PDX-MI puts patient treatment history in its Clinical/Patient module and model drug dosing and response in a separate Model Study module. An iScience 2025 study of colorectal cancer organoids likewise uses 'pretreated' to mean the patient had chemotherapy before the organoid was derived. I found no cBioPortal page that defines THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION itself. The #-prefixed description line for that column in the study's data_clinical_sample.txt is the deciding check. Either way, the field does not measure how engrafted tumoroids responded in mice.
